**THE LAST OF THE NOBLEST GENERATION**

Harry Patch, the last survivor of the First World War, and the man who reminded the modern world of its obscene massacre, died at the age of 111. His life ended on a fine summer morning in his native Somerset, many miles from the Belgian land of Ypres where so many of his comrades fell, and where he so nearly joined them. For decades he kept the sights and sounds of that terrible experience to himself. But then, at the age of 100, he began to talk…

Born in the village of Coombe Down, Harry left school at 14 for an apprenticeship with a plumber, and would, no doubt, have lived a life of peaceful anonymity if the war hadn’t been declared. Being too young at first, at the age of 17 Harry was **conscripted**. “I didn’t want to go and fight anyone, but it was a case of having to,” he said. He was in charge of a machine gun, and, by his 19th birthday, was in a **trench** in the middle of one of the most famous and bloodiest battles of the First World War: the Battle of Ypres. “Anyone who tells you he wasn’t **scared** is a damned liar,” Harry would later say. “We lived by the hour… You saw the sun rise; hopefully, you’d see it set. If you saw it set, you hoped you’d see it rise.”

Many didn’t. One of them was a young soldier whom Patch and his comrades found in the battlefield, badly wounded by **shrapnel**. “Shoot me,” he said, and then, before Harry could react, he died with the words “Mother!” on his lips. It was but one of the phantoms from the trenches that Harry carried with him until his death. Later on, in September 1917, came the German projectile which would hit Harry. It burst among his **mates** with such force that three of them were never found again. Harry, some metres away, was seriously wounded, his stomach pierced by shrapnel. He was taken to a **CCS (casualty clearing station)**, where he lay, untreated in maddening pain, for one day and a half. Finally, a doctor came, and, with no anaesthetic, took out the metal while four men held him down. Although he would not be **demobbed** for another year, that was the end of Harry’s war. He returned home, to plumbing, marriage, two sons, and an old age that saw him survive both sons and his wife.

All this time, he had kept those memories of war to himself, telling no one. But then, as he passed his 100th birthday, a journalist called Richard Emden asked Harry if he would talk of war. He agreed and he wrote, with Richard’s help, his life story, and became a witness for those comrades who had been killed so many years before. When Richard Emden went to see him, Harry sat at a table in the morning room of his house. The conversation went mainly one-way. Harry’s mind was sharp, and his sight good, but his voice was soft and delicate, and he was practically speechless. The journalist ended the interview before he had intended, afraid to be more of an inconvenience than he had already been.

His voice and body may have died, but his words on war should live on, resonating strongly. Harry Patch had words for all his experiences. They were spoken with an anger that lasted all his adult life. “War,” he said, “is organised murder, and nothing else.”

*Text adapted from The Independent (July 26, 2009)*

**1.** Which of the following sentences about Harry Patch is FALSE?

opcions.A: He was the only survivor of the First World War.
opcions.B: He only explained his experiences when he was 100.
opcions.C: He nearly died during the Battle of Ypres.
opcions.D: He died at the age of 111 in his home country.

passos.cos: Pregunta de **reading** de resposta única (Part 1). Llegeix primer l'enunciat i les quatre opcions, localitza al text el paràgraf on se'n parla i compara-hi cada opció. Val **0,5 punts** si l'encertes, però **resta 0,16 si falles** i no resta res si la deixes en blanc: si només n'has pogut descartar una, potser val més deixar-la; si n'has descartat dues, val la pena respondre. Compte amb els distractors que copien paraules del text però en canvien el sentit. Atenció: aquesta pregunta demana l'afirmació **FALSA**; les altres tres són certes segons el text.

Paràgraf 1: *“Harry Patch, **the last survivor** of the First World War”*. Ser *l'últim supervivent* (el darrer que quedava viu) no vol dir ser *l'únic* (*the only survivor*): molts altres soldats van sobreviure, però ell va ser el que va morir més tard. Per tant, A és **falsa**.

- C és certa: *“the Belgian land of Ypres where so many of his comrades fell, and where **he so nearly joined them**”* (gairebé hi mor).
- D és certa: *“died at the age of 111 [...] in his native Somerset”*.

**A. He was the only survivor of the First World War.** The text says Harry Patch was “the last survivor of the First World War”, which means he was the last one still alive, not the only one who survived. All the other options are true.

**THE LAST OF THE NOBLEST GENERATION**

Harry Patch, the last survivor of the First World War, and the man who reminded the modern world of its obscene massacre, died at the age of 111. His life ended on a fine summer morning in his native Somerset, many miles from the Belgian land of Ypres where so many of his comrades fell, and where he so nearly joined them. For decades he kept the sights and sounds of that terrible experience to himself. But then, at the age of 100, he began to talk…

Born in the village of Coombe Down, Harry left school at 14 for an apprenticeship with a plumber, and would, no doubt, have lived a life of peaceful anonymity if the war hadn’t been declared. Being too young at first, at the age of 17 Harry was **conscripted**. “I didn’t want to go and fight anyone, but it was a case of having to,” he said. He was in charge of a machine gun, and, by his 19th birthday, was in a **trench** in the middle of one of the most famous and bloodiest battles of the First World War: the Battle of Ypres. “Anyone who tells you he wasn’t **scared** is a damned liar,” Harry would later say. “We lived by the hour… You saw the sun rise; hopefully, you’d see it set. If you saw it set, you hoped you’d see it rise.”

Many didn’t. One of them was a young soldier whom Patch and his comrades found in the battlefield, badly wounded by **shrapnel**. “Shoot me,” he said, and then, before Harry could react, he died with the words “Mother!” on his lips. It was but one of the phantoms from the trenches that Harry carried with him until his death. Later on, in September 1917, came the German projectile which would hit Harry. It burst among his **mates** with such force that three of them were never found again. Harry, some metres away, was seriously wounded, his stomach pierced by shrapnel. He was taken to a **CCS (casualty clearing station)**, where he lay, untreated in maddening pain, for one day and a half. Finally, a doctor came, and, with no anaesthetic, took out the metal while four men held him down. Although he would not be **demobbed** for another year, that was the end of Harry’s war. He returned home, to plumbing, marriage, two sons, and an old age that saw him survive both sons and his wife.

All this time, he had kept those memories of war to himself, telling no one. But then, as he passed his 100th birthday, a journalist called Richard Emden asked Harry if he would talk of war. He agreed and he wrote, with Richard’s help, his life story, and became a witness for those comrades who had been killed so many years before. When Richard Emden went to see him, Harry sat at a table in the morning room of his house. The conversation went mainly one-way. Harry’s mind was sharp, and his sight good, but his voice was soft and delicate, and he was practically speechless. The journalist ended the interview before he had intended, afraid to be more of an inconvenience than he had already been.

His voice and body may have died, but his words on war should live on, resonating strongly. Harry Patch had words for all his experiences. They were spoken with an anger that lasted all his adult life. “War,” he said, “is organised murder, and nothing else.”

*Text adapted from The Independent (July 26, 2009)*

problemes.titol: Carta d'un soldat de la Primera Guerra Mundial als seus pares
problemes.enunciat:
Choose ONE topic. Write about number 1 or 2. Minimum length: 100 words.

[4 points]

**Topic 1.** Imagine that you are a soldier in the First World War. Write a letter to your parents about your experiences in the war.

passos.cos: Opció 1 del writing (cal triar-ne una de les dues): una **carta informal** als pares, en primera persona i escrita *des del front*, mínim 100 paraules (apunta a 150-180, uns 25-30 minuts). Cal que expliquis **experiències** (què veus, com vius, què sents). El registre és familiar però correcte: contraccions permeses, to afectuós. Està relacionat amb el reading (Harry Patch), i en pots aprofitar el context (trinxeres, Ypres, metralla), però **no copiïs** frases del text: es penalitza. Compte amb els anacronismes (res de mòbils ni correus electrònics!).

Estructura de la carta:

1. **Salutació** (*Dear Mum and Dad,*) i obertura afectuosa: com estan, on ets.
2. **Descripció de la vida al front**: condicions (fang, pluja, rates, soroll), rutines.
3. **Una experiència concreta** narrada en passat (un atac, un company ferit): dona-li emoció.
4. **Tranquil·litzar els pares** i parlar del futur (tornar a casa).
5. **Comiat** (*With all my love, / Love,*) i signatura.

**Estructures i connectors útils**

- Temps verbals: *present perfect* (*we have been here for three weeks*), *present continuous* (*I am writing from...*), *past simple* per a fets concrets (*a shell exploded*), *will* / *hope* per al futur.
- Connectors: *though, however, so, so that, because, which (relatiu), not even*.
- Expressions de carta informal: *I hope you are both well, Please don't worry, Give my love to..., I miss you*.
- Comparacions que llueixen: *as big as cats, like brothers, nothing like the posters promised*.

Dear Mum and Dad,

I hope you are both well and that the farm is not too hard without me. I am writing from a muddy trench near Ypres, where we have been for almost three weeks.

Life here is nothing like the posters promised. It rains every day, our boots are always wet and the rats are as big as cats. The worst thing, though, is the noise of the guns, which never stops, not even at night. Last Tuesday a shell exploded near our position and my friend Tom was badly wounded. I still cannot stop thinking about him.

Please don't worry too much. I am being careful and the lads here look after each other like brothers. Your letters and Mum's cake have kept me going, so please keep writing.

I really hope this war will be over soon, so that I can come home and help you with the harvest next summer.

With all my love,

John

problemes.enunciat:
Choose ONE topic. Write about number 1 or 2. Minimum length: 100 words.

[4 points]

**Topic 2.** Harry Patch did not explain his experiencies about the war until he was very elderly. Why do you think he waited for so many years? Write an opinion essay about it for your local paper.

passos.cos: Opció 2 del writing (cal triar-ne una de les dues): un **opinion essay** per al diari local, mínim 100 paraules (apunta a 150-180, uns 25-30 minuts). La pregunta és concreta: **per què** creus que va esperar tants anys? Cal donar raons pròpies (hipòtesis raonades), no resumir el text. Registre neutre-formal: evita contraccions i expressions massa col·loquials. Pots referir-te al reading, però **no copiïs** frases senceres. (L'enunciat de l'examen diu *experiencies*, una errada tipogràfica per *experiences*.)

Estructura en 4-5 paràgrafs:

1. **Introducció**: presenta el fet (Harry Patch, l'últim supervivent, no va parlar fins als 100 anys) i anuncia la teva opinió.
2. **Raó 1**: el dolor dels records (trauma, no voler reviure-ho).
3. **Raó 2**: el context social (els homes no expressaven sentiments; ningú parlava de salut mental).
4. **Raó 3**: en ser l'últim, sentia la responsabilitat de ser testimoni.
5. **Conclusió**: resumeix i valora.

**Estructures i connectors útils**

- Opinió: *In my opinion, I believe that, I think that, It seems to me that*.
- Ordenar arguments: *First of all, Secondly, Finally, Moreover, What is more*.
- Conclusió: *To sum up, In conclusion, All in all*.
- Gramàtica que llueix: *would have + participi* (*talking about it would have meant...*), passiva (*were expected to*, *were not encouraged to*), *past perfect* (*he had seen*), segon condicional (*If he did not speak, ... would be lost*), *although*.

**Why did Harry Patch wait so long to speak?**

Harry Patch, the last survivor of the First World War, did not talk about his experiences until he was 100 years old. Why did he keep silent for so long? In my opinion, there are several reasons.

First of all, I believe the memories were simply too painful. He had seen friends die in front of him, and talking about it would have meant living through it all again. Many soldiers preferred to forget and concentrate on their families and jobs.

Secondly, people at that time were not encouraged to show their feelings. Men were expected to be strong, and nobody spoke about mental health or trauma.

Finally, I think that when he became very old, he realised he was the last witness. If he did not speak, the voices of his comrades would be lost forever.

To sum up, although his silence is understandable, I am glad he finally spoke, because his words remind us that war is never the answer.

**Interviewer:** And what does the training consist of?

**Julie:** First the dogs need to be socialised when they are very young, between 3 and 8 weeks. These puppies stay with a volunteer for a full-time socialisation period of about one year: they get exposed to a wide range of people, animals, places and experiences. Then they arrive in the organisation for their sound training and are allocated to a trainer, such as myself.

**Interviewer:** These dogs have a little dark red jacket on, which tells you that they are hearing dogs. Why do they wear them?

**Julie:** Well, this is because the problem for a lot of deaf people is that their disability is invisible. If you’re blind there are obvious indications because you would be walking with a stick, but with hearing loss, it is very difficult to tell, and that can cause a lot of problems.

**Interviewer:** You are right… I never thought of this!

**Julie:** It’s actually a serious problem. Many of the hearing aids that people use now are so small that they can’t be seen, so you don’t know whether a person who has hearing loss is perhaps struggling with it in many social situations.

**Interviewer:** Could you give us an example?

**Julie:** Sure! Many of our clients comment on how they are often in supermarkets and people behind them would say: “Excuse me, do you mind moving to the side?” because they are there with their shopping trolley. But they don’t hear the comment and do nothing and people often think they are rude, but of course they just didn’t hear the comment.

**Interviewer:** I see…

**Julie:** So the dog makes a huge difference in that situation, because it stands next to the person with its hearing dog jacket on, telling everybody in the shop that the person with the dog is deaf, and therefore it starts to break down some of those barriers created by deafness.

**Interviewer:** I see… It is very important that the dogs wear these jackets. How many hearing dogs can the charity provide? How many are available?

**Julie:** At the moment we have slightly more than 800 deaf people allocated to one of our dogs across the UK, but since we started we have trained 1,850 dogs, so we have got a long history working with people, but we can never provide enough dogs.

**Interviewer:** That’s excellent! But, at a personal level, do you find your job rewarding?

**Julie:** Yes, definitely! I have worked for the Charity for nearly seven years now so there have been lots of good moments! I also find it really rewarding speaking to dog owners and seeing how much their hearing dogs have changed their lives.

**Interviewer:** What is it like to work with other trainers that might have different ideas about how to best train a dog?

**Julie:** Everyone is here to help improve the lives of deaf people, and so all the staff and volunteers are like one big team. Like any job, there are difficult moments too, but a sweet puppy or a ball game with one of the dogs soon puts a smile back on your face!

**Interviewer:** What are you working on at the moment?

**Julie:** I am currently training four dogs and have another one coming in next week, so that keeps me pretty busy. The job is full of variety though, which I love. One day you can be training sound work and the next you can be taking a dog on the train to London. It is important that each dog is well adapted, matched to their owner’s lifestyle so we prepare them as much as we can.

**Interviewer:** A truly fascinating job! Julie, thank you for telling us about it. I’m afraid we’ve run out of time. Thank you so much for being with us today!

**Julie:** It was a pleasure! Thank you.
